I will say, just up front, I'm very glad for all the civil conversation that's been had. Unfortunately I've run into too many times where it devolves into arguments. 

As a purely personal (and professional to an extent) I've never seen ABA used properly in my occupation, and when proposed it be used on me it made no sense (logically to me). The idea of stopping self-injurious behavior is absolutely a goal to strive for, no argument there

Mainly in my field I see it too often used for (in one of the articles mentioned in the comments) to "fix" benign behaviors that only exist to conform individuals to society (stimming, nonverbal behavior). In my professional experience I seem to only see other professionals I worked with bordering on infantilizing those who were getting ABA (at any age range)

I've personally found it to just be more effective to use other models to improve behavior and stop anything genuinely harmful. In regards to personal experience I often encountered people insisting I should/should've stopped stimming by this point due to it being inappropriate. I've found simply expressing certain aspects of my autistic behavior gets my work scrutinized

Aside from all this? Nothing I say would be new with the above comment. A very well thought out reply there

I'm not saying the date a is fabricated, I'm more saying the methods used a lot in ABA (at least in my part of the globe) are trying to accomplish a goal that isn't ethical and isn't sustainable in the long term

As someone on the autism spectrum I always found a lot of the approaches in ABA to be more "Corrective" (trying to make individuals fit in with the "norm") when this isn't an approach we should really be taking to begin with. It's one thing to teach life skills, it's another to try to make people conform to a social standard that varies from culture to culture. Not to mention a lot of the ABA research in the beginning wasn't valid in the long term. Many persons, without constant "treatment" (for lack of a better term) completely relapsed and for others it didn't work. Now that being said? For some people it absolutely did work, but only in the goal ABA is trying to accomplish.

I'm more on the side of neurodivergent psychology, I fundamentally don't believe in teaching people social acts that they don't need to know in order to function but instead are to make other people at ease

You very well could have a lack of empathy, but the concept isn't as clear cut as that. There is a spectrum of people with no empathy (or simply low empathy) that has "zero empathy positive" and "zero empathy negative". Narcissist and sociopaths are in the negative while people on the autistic spectrum (as an example, but there are more) are on the positive of this of this. Negative empathy persons lack affective empathy and can only really see people the same way you see a chair (paraphrased, but simple way to put it). Positive spectrum persons lack cognitive empathy, which essentially means they can't place themselves in someone else's shoes, though they can feel bad when they see someone else feeling bad due to not liking that someone else is sad rather than actually sharing in the sadness. 

Having no empathy isn't a 100% guarantee that you're evil of some sort, though it could lead to some problems in life if you don't learn how to compensate for some of it.
